§2.1a — Constellations

Unit 2: The Night Sky · Astronomy

Go outside at about 9 pm next week and look east. A bright red star comes up first, then three stars in a perfectly straight row, then a brilliant blue-white star below them. That is Orion, the Hunter, and the fuzzy pink patch under the row is a cloud where new stars are being born.

On a dark night you can see about 3000 stars at once. How do astronomers keep track of them all, and how do you say exactly where one is, so that someone across the world can point a telescope at it?

Today: the constellations, the celestial sphere, and the address of every star (RA and Dec).

Orion. Photo: Akira Fujii, via ESA/Hubble (CC BY 4.0)

Constellations

People have always grouped the bright stars into pictures. Those groups are the constellations. The Greeks saw Orion as a hunter, with a raised club, a shield, and a belt of three stars. Before you see anyone else's picture, make your own.

Orion: connect the dots, then compare
Explore around Orion in skymap ↗
Click one star, then another, to draw a line between them. Draw your own figure first.

Your figure and Rey's are both fine. A constellation's stick figure is just a way to remember it; what you have to know for the Night Sky quiz is where it is, its outline, and its abbreviation (Orion is Ori).

Measure: how tall is Orion?

Use the Dec lines on the chart. Read the declination of Betelgeuse (the red shoulder) and of Rigel (the blue foot), and subtract. About how many degrees of declination does Orion span from Betelgeuse to Rigel?

degrees
Look up. On Tue Nov 3, Orion's belt rises due east at about 8:56 pm from Portland and is highest, due south, at about 2:53 am. Each night it rises about 4 minutes earlier, so by early December it is up before 7 pm. (Computed for Portland with Astronomy Engine.)

Careful! Close in the sky is not close in space

We see the stars as if they had no depth, all painted on the same dome. Orion's stars only look close together because they lie in nearly the same direction. Their distances are very different.

Turn Orion sideways
Predict first: which is closest to us?
Earth
Make your prediction first. Then drag the slider to fly around and look at Orion from the side.

Seen from the side, the Hunter falls apart. One shoulder, Bellatrix, is about 250 light-years away; the Belt stars are about 1,300, five times farther. A constellation is a direction in the sky, not a group of neighbours.

Measure: when did Betelgeuse's light leave?

Betelgeuse is about 550 light-years away. Light travels one light-year in one year. In about what year did the light you see tonight leave Betelgeuse?

year

Distances are rounded, and the same ones skymap uses.

88 constellations, which take up area

Since 1930 the International Astronomical Union has divided the whole sky into 88 constellations, with official borders like the states on a map. A constellation is not just its stick figure; it is an area of sky. Every star, galaxy and nebula lies inside exactly one of them.

The whole sky, flattened: click anywhere
First, find Orion: click where you think Orion's area is. (Hint: it sits on the blue line.)
Close-up
Explore in skymap ↗

The map is the whole sky unrolled, like a world map. Left to right is Right Ascension, top to bottom is Declination, and the blue line is the celestial equator. The next tiles explain all three.

Measure: which constellation?

A comet is spotted at RA $= 5^{\rm h}$, Dec $= +45^\circ$. Find that spot on the map (the readout shows where your mouse is). Which constellation is the comet in? Type its name or abbreviation.

The Celestial Sphere

To help understand how the stars move, astronomers invented the celestial sphere: pretend every star is stuck to a huge sphere with Earth at its centre. Three things on it come straight from Earth:

  • Celestial Equator (CE): Earth's equator projected onto the celestial sphere.
  • North Celestial Pole (NCP): the point directly above Earth's spin axis, out past the North Pole.
  • South Celestial Pole (SCP): the point directly below Earth's spin axis.
Earth inside the celestial sphere: drag to turn the view
View:

The stars are not really moving. We now know that the rotation of the Earth causes the sky to appear to move. Every star circles the NCP once a day, and the closer it is to the pole, the smaller its circle. The star near the NCP is Polaris, the North Star.

Measure: how close is Polaris to the pole?

Polaris has a declination of $\delta = +89.26^\circ$, and the NCP is at $+90^\circ$. How many degrees is Polaris from the NCP? The Moon is about $0.5^\circ$ across; how many Moon-widths is that?

degrees

The Equatorial System

How do you find the location of a city? Longitude is east or west of the Prime Meridian; latitude is north or south of the Equator.

How do you find the location of a star? The same way, on the celestial sphere: Right Ascension is like longitude and Declination is like latitude.

RA = Right Ascension ($\alpha$). Given in time units, e.g. $\alpha = 12^{\rm h}34^{\rm m}56^{\rm s}$. There are $24^{\rm h}$ in the complete celestial sphere, so $1^{\rm h} = 15^\circ$. RA $= 0^{\rm h}$ is the First Point of Aries, ♈ (the vernal equinox).

Dec = Declination ($\delta$). Given in degrees, arcminutes and arcseconds, e.g. $\delta = +12^\circ 34' 56''$. Celestial Equator $= 0^\circ$, NCP $= +90^\circ$, SCP $= -90^\circ$.

The Sun's yearly path around the sky is the ecliptic. It is tilted $23.5^\circ$ to the celestial equator, because Earth's axis is tilted. The two lines cross at ♈, where RA starts, and again at $12^{\rm h}$. (Remember from §1.4b: the Moon's orbit is tilted another $5^\circ$ from the ecliptic.)

You already know this on Earth. Turn the Earth and click anywhere for its latitude and longitude. Then turn the sky: the grid is the same idea, with Dec for latitude and RA for longitude.

On Earth: latitude and longitude
Portland is at about 45.5° N, 122.7° W. Click anywhere on the Earth.
In the sky: Dec and RA
Hour lines run pole to pole and are labelled along the celestial equator. Click a star. A globe shows the sky from outside, so it is mirrored: RA increases to the right here, but to the left on a star chart, which shows the sky as we see it from inside.

Where the analogy breaks. Longitude is fixed to the Earth and counts degrees east or west of Greenwich. RA is fixed to the stars, counts eastward from ♈ all the way around, and is measured in hours: $0^{\rm h}$ to $24^{\rm h}$. As the Earth spins, every longitude passes under every hour of RA once a day.

Astronomical Angles

$$\text{Whole circle} = 360^\circ$$ $$1^\circ = 60'\ \text{(arcminutes)} \qquad 1' = 60''\ \text{(arcseconds)}$$ To go to decimal degrees, divide arcminutes by 60 and arcseconds by 3600. For RA, turn hours into decimal hours the same way, then multiply by 15.
Zoom into one degree
Ex. 1
Ex. 4 · Convert (21h45m, +63°15′) to decimal degrees
Reveal
$$\alpha = 21 + \frac{45}{60} = 21.75^{\rm h}, \qquad 21.75^{\rm h} \times 15\,\frac{^\circ}{^{\rm h}} = \boxed{326.25^\circ}$$ $$\delta = 63 + \frac{15}{60} = \boxed{+63.25^\circ}$$

Betelgeuse is at $\alpha = 5^{\rm h}55^{\rm m}10^{\rm s}$, $\delta = +7^\circ 24' 25''$. Convert both to decimal degrees.
